title: 10 ways to use Semrush historical data (with examples)
summary: Learn 10 ways to use Semrush historical data to diagnose traffic drops, track keyword ranking history, spot seasonality, and research AI visibility.
body_markdown:
Historical SEO data lets you look back at past keyword rankings, traffic changes, and competitor growth. Semrush historical data gives you estimates of all three, month by month, for almost any domain or keyword.


But a traffic chart that dips doesn't tell you much on its own.


Was it a Google update? A seasonal slowdown? A drop every site in your niche felt? Or a problem on your site that needs fixing?


This guide walks through 10 workflows that help you answer those questions in Semrush. You'll learn how to diagnose traffic drops, review keyword ranking history, check historical search engine results page (SERP) data, separate real trends from seasonality, and see when sites started appearing in AI Overviews.


## Why SEO data without history is a guess


SEO data without history is a guess because a single month shows you what happened but not whether it matters.


Say your estimated organic traffic fell 20% last month. That number alone can't tell you whether to rewrite pages, fix a technical issue, or wait it out.


Historical data can. It lets you check a change against the three things behind most false alarms:


- **Seasonality** : Many keywords rise and fall on a yearly cycle. A February dip is normal if it happens every February.
- **Industry-wide shifts** : Google updates and changes in demand hit whole niches at once. If your competitors fell in the same month, the cause probably isn't your site.
- **SERP changes** : New[AI Overviews](https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-overviews-traffic-loss/) , ads, and other[SERP features](https://www.semrush.com/blog/serp-features-guide/) can push organic results down even when your rankings hold.


Here's an example from the recipe niche:


From August to September 2025, Allrecipes, Simply Recipes, Serious Eats, and Delish each lost between 11% and 24% of their estimated organic traffic. Every site fell in the same month, so the cause was likely outside any one of them.


Then, from January to October 2026, Simply Recipes lost about 55% of its estimated traffic. Over the same months, Allrecipes and Delish held roughly flat, and Serious Eats grew 44%.


Same metric. Same niche. Two very different stories.


The first drop called for patience. The second called for an investigation. That's the idea behind every workflow in this guide: Don't make decisions based on a number until you know its history.


## What is Semrush historical data?


Semrush historical data is a record of past SEO metrics, such as rankings, organic traffic, and search volume, for almost any domain or keyword, stored month by month back to January 2012.


In practice, you pick a past month in a tool's date selector, and the report shows what it looked like back then. That gives you the "before" picture for any change you're trying to explain.


Here's the historical SEO data you can pull for a past month:


- **Domain metrics** : Estimated organic traffic, ranking keywords, and top pages in[Domain Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/overview/) and[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/)
- **Historical keyword rankings** : Which keywords a domain ranked for, and how positions moved, in Organic Rankings' "Position Changes" report
- **Keyword metrics** : Historical search volume, keyword difficulty, intent, and the SERP for a single term in[Keyword Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordoverview/)
- **Competitor overlap** : Shared and missing keywords between domains at a past date in[Keyword Gap](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordgap/)


How far back you can go depends on the regional database. The U.S. and eight other core databases start in January 2012, while newer regional databases start in December 2013 or December 2016.[Position Tracking](https://www.semrush.com/position-tracking/) works differently: It stores daily rankings for 60 days and weekly rankings for up to 140 weeks, starting from the day you create a campaign.


***Further reading*** *: For the full breakdown by tool and database, see our*[knowledge base article on available historical data](https://www.semrush.com/kb/64-historical-data) *.*


Historical data comes with Guru-level SEO Toolkit access (Semrush One Pro+ and up, or SEO Classic Guru and Business).


Keep in mind that these figures are estimates of monthly averages. They're built to show direction and turning points, so pair them with your own analytics when you need exact numbers.


## How to use Semrush historical data


You can use Semrush historical data to explain traffic changes, find content worth refreshing, study how competitors grew, separate trends from seasonality, and track your visibility in AI Search over time. Each workflow below starts with the general question it answers, then shows how to find that answer in Semrush.


### 1. Diagnose SEO traffic drops


To diagnose an SEO traffic drop, find the month it started, then check whether it lines up with a Google update, a change on your site, a change on the SERP, or a drop across your whole niche.


Start in[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) :


1. Enter your domain and stay on the " **Overview** " tab
2. Click the " **Traffic** " metric to open the "Estimated Traffic Trend" chart
3. Set the range to " **2Y** " or " **All time** " so you can see when the decline began and whether it has happened before


Note the month the drop started. Then, check whether it lines up with a[Google update](https://www.semrush.com/blog/google-algorithm-update/) .


Open[Domain Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/overview/) for the same domain, set the chart to " **All time** " and " **Months** ," and look for the Google update markers (the small "G" icons along the bottom of the "Keywords" chart).


The " **Notes** " menu above the "Traffic" chart lets you show confirmed and unconfirmed updates, plus your own notes about site changes like migrations, redesigns, or launches.


Next, check whether the drop is industry-wide.


Open[Compare Domains](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/comparedomains/) and add your domain plus up to four competitors. Compare their organic traffic over the same months.


If your competitors fell in the same month, the cause is likely outside your site, like the shared August to September 2025 dip across the recipe sites earlier in this guide. If only your site fell, keep digging.


Finally, find the keywords behind the drop. Back in Organic Rankings, go to the " **Position Changes** " tab and switch the "Position Changes Trend" chart to " **Monthly** ." Then click the " **Changes on SERP** " card to filter for keywords where the results page itself changed.


The "Changes on SERP" column shows which SERP features appeared or disappeared for each keyword.


Here's how to read what you find:


- **Competitors dropped too** : The cause is likely an algorithm update or a shift in demand. Check whether the pattern repeats each year (see workflow 5) before you change anything.
- **Only you dropped, with SERP changes** : New SERP features may be pushing your pages down. The next workflow shows how to see exactly what changed.
- **Only you dropped, with no SERP changes** : The problem is probably on your pages. They may be outdated or outranked, so[update and optimize them](https://www.semrush.com/blog/when-to-update-blog-content/) to win back lost ground.


### 2. See historical SERP data for a keyword


Historical SERP data shows which pages ranked for a keyword in a past month and which SERP features appeared, so you can see exactly how a results page changed.


It's the fastest way to explain a lost position. Sometimes the SERP around your pages simply changed, and that caused the drop.


Use[Keyword Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordoverview/) to see SERP historical data:


1. Enter a keyword and pick your country database
2. Click the date selector next to the device menu (it shows today's date) and choose a month under "Historical Data"
3. Scroll down to "SERP Analysis" to see the top 100 results and the SERP features for that month
4. Switch the date back to today and compare the two views


Here's an example for "air fryer recipes" in the U.S. database:


In October 2024, the SERP had no AI Overview. Skinnytaste ranked first with an estimated 45,900 monthly visits from search, and Allrecipes and Delish both held top 10 spots.


By November 2026, an AI Overview and a video carousel had joined the page. Skinnytaste's page had slipped to 10th with about 6,600 estimated visits, and neither Allrecipes nor Delish ranked in the top 10 anymore.


So, if you owned one of those pages, rewriting the content wouldn't fix everything. The new SERP layout likely sends fewer clicks to organic results, too.


When you compare two months, look for:


- **New SERP features** : AI Overviews, video carousels, or forums that push organic results down the page
- **New types of pages** : Category pages, listicles, or community threads replacing the format you rank with
- **New competitors** : Sites that entered the top 10, which are worth studying with workflow 4


Then, decide what to change. A new format usually means updating your page to match what's ranking now. A new SERP feature might mean targeting that feature directly, like adding a video for a keyword that now shows a video carousel.


### 3. Use keyword ranking history to find content worth reviving


Keyword ranking history shows which keywords a page used to rank for and where it ranks now, so you can spot content that's slipping before it stops sending traffic.


These pages are often your best refresh candidates. They've already proven they can rank, and they usually need less work to recover than a new page needs to rank from scratch.


1. Enter your domain and open the " **Position Changes** " tab
2. Set the date range to cover the months you want to review (up to two years)
3. Click the " **Declined** " card to show only keywords that lost positions
4. Sort by " **Traffic Diff.** " so the keywords that cost you the most traffic rise to the top


Check the "Diff." column for big position drops, and the URL column for pages that show up again and again. When several declining keywords point to the same URL, that page is losing traction.


Next, confirm the decline at the page level in[Top Pages](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/toppages/) :


1. Enter your domain
2. Use the " **Date** " selector to pick a month when your traffic was higher
3. Note your top URLs and their estimated traffic
4. Switch back to the current month and compare


Here's what that looks like for Simply Recipes, the site from the example earlier in this guide:


In January 2026, its top page was a roundup of easy dinner recipes, with an estimated 281,400 monthly visits. Its top keyword was "recipes."


By November 2026, the same page brought in about 1,300 visits, and its top keyword had changed to "what to cook easy." In other words, the page lost its ranking for a broad, high-volume term and kept only a much smaller one.


Pages that fell furthest down the search results page — or lost the most traffic — go to the top of your refresh queue.


Before you rewrite anything, open a lost keyword in[Keyword Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordoverview/) and look at what ranks today in the "SERP Analysis" section. Visit a few of the top results and note how they're structured, which subtopics they cover, and how current their information is.


Then, switch the date to the month your page started slipping.


If the same pages still rank and the layout hasn’t changed, your content fell behind. Update it with what you learned from the pages that now outrank it. If new SERP features or a different type of page took over, then the SERP itself changed, and a rewrite alone won't win the traffic back (see workflow 2).


Either way, the SERP's history tells you which fix you need.


### 4. Study a competitor's website ranking history


Website ranking history shows how a competitor's organic traffic, ranking keywords, and top pages changed month by month, so you can[pinpoint when they grew and what drove it](https://www.semrush.com/blog/how-to-do-seo-competitive-analysis/) .


You can see:


- When their estimated organic traffic rose or fell
- Which pages gained visibility first
- Which keywords they ranked for in any given month
- Whether they grew by publishing more pages or by consolidating fewer, stronger ones


1. Enter a competitor's domain
2. Click the " **Traffic** " metric and set the range to " **2Y** " or " **All time** "
3. Look for clear periods of growth or decline, and note the months they started


Then, open[Top Pages](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/toppages/) for the same domain. Use the " **Date** " selector to view a month before the change, then a month after it, and compare which URLs drove traffic in each.


Here's an example. Serious Eats' estimated organic traffic grew from about 10.8 million in March 2026 to 16.8 million in July 2026.


In July, its top page was a roundup of 30-minute dinners, with about 242,000 estimated monthly visits and "easy dinner ideas" as its top keyword.


In March, that URL didn't appear in Top Pages at all.


Over the same months, the site's organic page count barely moved, from about 13,600 to 13,900. So, the growth didn't come from publishing more. It came from a few new pages winning broad, high-volume queries.


What can we draw from this? If you compete with Serious Eats, its growth came from a handful of well-built pages on broad topics, not from adding more pages. And it's the same topic where Simply Recipes' easy-dinners roundup lost most of its traffic in 2026, which makes "easy dinner ideas" a SERP worth watching.


Keep an eye on the "Organic Pages" line in Top Pages, too. When a competitor's page count drops while its traffic holds or rises, it has likely[removed thin pages or consolidated similar content](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-pruning/) .


Before you copy a competitor's move, check what happened to the SERPs they won. Open one of their new top keywords in Keyword Overview and compare a month before their growth with a month after, as in workflow 2.


If your competitor’s page simply outranked the old results, they did something worth learning from. If a SERP feature disappeared or Google started favoring a different type of page, the SERP did most of the work, and copying their page won't get you the same result. Their traffic chart alone can’t tell you which.


Finally, see which keywords a competitor gained with[Keyword Gap](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordgap/) :


1. Enter your domain and up to four competitors
2. Use the date selector to pick a month before the competitor's growth
3. Review the keywords they ranked for that you didn't
4. Switch to the current month and see which new keywords they've added since


The keywords that appear only in the recent view show where the competitor has expanded, and which topics you may need to cover next.


### 5. Separate real keyword trends from seasonality


To separate real keyword trends from seasonality, run two checks. First, check the shape of the "Trend" chart to see whether a keyword is seasonal and when it peaks. Then, compare "Volume" for the same month across different years to see whether demand is really growing or shrinking.


You need both because of how Semrush calculates "Volume." The figure you see for any month is the average of the 12 months leading up to it, so the yearly cycle is already averaged out. Two months from the same year will show nearly the same volume, even for a very seasonal keyword. The same month in different years, though, compares two full, separate years of demand.


Use[Keyword Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordoverview/) to check historical search volume:


1. Enter the keyword you're evaluating
2. Click the date selector and pick a month, such as October 2023
3. Note the "Volume," "Keyword Difficulty," and "Intent" figures, and look at the "Trend" chart
4. Repeat for the same month in each following year


The "Trend" chart breaks that average back into the 12 months behind it, so you can see whether interest holds steady or spikes at certain times of year.


Here's how two keywords compare across three Octobers in the U.S. database:


**Keyword**


**October 2023**


**October 2024**


**October 2025**


halloween costumes


550,000


550,000


550,000


air fryer recipes


110,000


74,000


135,000


"Halloween costumes" is pure seasonality. Its "Trend" chart packs almost all of its searches into a few months, but its average volume hasn't moved in three years, so overall demand is steady.


"Air fryer recipes" tells a different story. Volume fell 33% from October 2023 to October 2024. Since each figure covers a full 12 months, seasonality can't explain the drop.


The October 2025 figure looks like a strong rebound. But its "Trend" chart shows one month spiking far above the other 11, and that single spike lifts the 12-month average. Today, the keyword's volume is back to about 90,500.


So, always check the "Trend" chart before you call a jump in volume a trend.


As you compare years, watch for:


- **Search volume changes** : A steady decline or climb in the same month, year after year
- [Search intent](https://www.semrush.com/blog/search-intent/) **changes** : A shift from informational to commercial, for example, which changes the type of page that ranks
- **Keyword Difficulty changes** : Higher or lower competition than when you last checked


Difficulty and intent can move as much as volume. "Air fryer recipes" had a[Keyword Difficulty](https://www.semrush.com/blog/keyword-difficulty/) of 82% in October 2023, 59% in October 2024, and 41% in October 2025, so it's far easier to rank for now than it was three years ago.


"Halloween costumes" shows the same drop in difficulty, from 88% to 55% over those three Octobers. Its intent changed too. In October 2023, Semrush labeled it informational and navigational. By October 2025, it was commercial, which means searchers now expect pages built to help them buy.


Together, these signals tell you whether a keyword is worth pursuing, whether it fits the content you have in mind, and whether you're likely to rank for it.


### 6. Use historical SEO data for AI visibility research


Historical SEO data shows when a site started appearing in[Google's AI Overviews](https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-overviews/) and how that presence has changed since, which gives you a longer view of AI visibility than most tracking tools can.


That longer view matters because[AI visibility tracking](https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-visibility/) usually starts the day you set it up. Historical SEO data lets you look back before that, for your own site or any competitor.


Use the "SERP Features Trend" chart in[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) :


1. Enter a domain and scroll down the " **Overview** " tab to "SERP Features Trend"
2. Uncheck " **Image pack** ," " **People also ask** ," and " **Discussions and Forums** "
3. Open the " **Other** " menu, click " **Deselect all** ," and check " **AI Overview** "
4. Set the range to " **2Y** " or " **All time** "


The chart now shows how many keywords had an AI Overview that linked to that domain, month by month.


Here's what it shows for reddit.com in the U.S. database:


Reddit first shows up as a linked AI Overview source in Semrush's data in September 2024, for just 575 keywords. By July 2025, that number had grown to about 7.2 million. It jumped again in spring 2026 and peaked at about 22.6 million keywords in May 2026. As of October 2026, it sat at about 16.8 million.


Run the same check on your own domain and your top competitors. Then, compare the timeline with your organic traffic from workflow 1. If your traffic dipped in the same months a competitor's AI Overview presence grew, you've found a likely reason.


Historical SEO data covers Google's AI Overviews. For a fuller picture of AI Search, two other tools help:


- [Position Tracking](https://www.semrush.com/position-tracking/) : Flags AI Overviews for the keywords you choose and can also track Google AI Mode and ChatGPT Search. It builds that history from the day you start a campaign.
- [AI Visibility Toolkit](https://www.semrush.com/ai-seo/overview/) : The "Visibility Overview" report shows how often AI platforms mention your brand, and it already includes backfilled history.


Prompt Tracking and Position Tracking can't fill in the past. Set them up now, so you'll have your own history the next time you need to explain a change.


### 7. Track your own keyword ranking history in Position Tracking


[Position Tracking](https://www.semrush.com/position-tracking/) records your own keyword ranking history from the day you create a campaign, giving you a more detailed record than monthly historical data can.


[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) estimates monthly positions for every keyword a site ranks for. Position Tracking checks the exact keywords, locations, and devices you choose, every day.


Here's how historical data in Position Tracking works:


- **Daily data** : Kept for 60 days
- **Weekly data** : Kept for 140 weeks after that, recorded on Wednesdays by default
- **Start date** : Collection begins the day you create the campaign, so you can't check rankings from before then
- **Competitors** : Any competitor you add later shows data back to the campaign's creation date


To view your keyword ranking history, open a Position Tracking campaign and change the date range at the top of the report. Dates older than 60 days appear grayed out in the calendar, since only weekly data points remain.


Once you have a few weeks of data, here's what to look for:


- **Many keywords dropping on the same day** : If your competitors fell too, it's likely an algorithm update. If only your site fell, check for a technical issue or site change from that week.
- **One page's keywords sliding slowly** : That page is falling behind and belongs in your refresh queue (see workflow 3)
- **Two of your URLs swapping places for the same keyword** : That's often keyword cannibalization, which the "Cannibalization" report flags
- **A competitor gaining on your most valuable keywords** : The "Competitors Discovery" report shows other sites ranking for the keywords in your campaign, including ones you haven't added yet


On any single day, all four look like a ranking drop. Your ranking history is what tells you which one you're dealing with, and whether it needs a fix or just time.


Since tracking can't go back in time, set it up right from day one. Track every keyword you'd hate to lose history for, including branded terms and the pages that drive revenue. Add your main competitors from the start, and choose the devices and locations your customers actually use.


Position Tracking also flags AI Overviews among the SERP features for your keywords. With access to the AI Visibility Toolkit, you can track Google AI Mode and ChatGPT Search in the same campaign.


***Further reading*** *:*[How do I see historical data in Position Tracking?](https://www.semrush.com/kb/1246-how-do-i-see-historical-data-in-position-tracking)


### 8. Create SEO reports with context


To create SEO reports with context, compare your current results against the same period in the past, then explain which changes drove the difference.


Year-over-year comparisons show leadership whether the work is paying off and which actions drove it. That proof of ROI is what justifies next quarter’s budget (or the team you already have).


For traffic, compare the same month across years to take seasonal swings out of the picture.


Then, open[Top Pages](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/toppages/) and use the " **Date** " selector to switch between the two periods.


Let's say you're reporting on Serious Eats for October 2026. In October 2025, the site had about 7.7 million estimated organic visits.


In October 2026, it had about 13.5 million, a 75% increase, with roughly the same number of ranking pages (about 14,500 vs. 14,400).


Comparing the two months shows where that growth came from:


- **Existing pages that grew** : The prime rib recipe went from about 27,600 visits to 114,300, and the no-bake cheesecake recipe from 37,600 to 62,900
- **New pages** : A food safety guide to chicken temperatures and the 30-minute dinners roundup, neither of which was among the site's top pages a year earlier, now bring in more than 60,000 visits each
- **Brand demand** : The homepage more than doubled, from about 44,200 visits to 103,500


In a report, that story might read like this:


*"Organic traffic is up 75% year over year, with about the same number of pages. Most of that growth came from updating pages that already ranked, plus two new high-value pages and stronger brand demand. Next quarter, we're doubling down on refreshes."*


To see which keywords fueled the change, go to[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) , open the " **Position Changes** " tab, and click the " **Improved** " card. It shows keywords where your rankings rose, plus keywords you've started ranking for.


Then, turn the comparison into a report leadership can read in[My Reports](https://www.semrush.com/my_reports/) :


1. Click " **Start from scratch** ," open " **Domain Analytics** " > " **Organic research** " in the widgets panel, and drag in widgets like "Organic Search: Summary," "Organic Search: Traffic / Keywords Chart," and "Organic Search: Top Pages"
2. At the top of the report, set " **Period** " to the month you're reporting on and " **Compare to** " to the same month a year earlier. Every widget linked to the report date updates to match
3. Open the " **Formatting** " panel and drag a " **Text** " block under each section. Use it to explain what you changed, which results stand out, and what's planned for next quarter
4. Click " **Generate PDF report** ," turn on " **Schedule report** ," and choose how often it goes out and who receives it


You can also[connect Google Analytics 4](https://www.semrush.com/blog/how-to-set-up-google-analytics/) and[Google Search Console](https://www.semrush.com/blog/google-search-console/) , so Semrush's estimates sit next to your own numbers. Once the report is scheduled, leadership sees the year-over-year picture every month, and each report adds to the record of what your SEO work has delivered.


***Further reading*** *:*[How to Create an SEO Report](https://www.semrush.com/blog/seo-report/)


### 9. Build custom reports with Semrush MCP


[Semrush MCP](https://www.semrush.com/kb/1618-mcp) (Model Context Protocol) lets you pull historical SEO data into an AI assistant with a plain-language prompt, so you can build custom reports without clicking through reports one month at a time.


MCP is a standard way for AI assistants to connect to outside data. Semrush MCP works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Notion, VS Code, and Claude Code.


To set it up:


1. Find Semrush in your AI assistant's app marketplace or integration settings (it's an official app in ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity)
2. Connect your Semrush account with OAuth or an API key
3. Ask for the data you need in plain language


Be specific about the domain, the country database, the metrics, and the months you want. For example:


*"Pull estimated monthly organic traffic and ranking keyword counts for seriouseats.com in the U.S. for each of the last 12 months. Then flag the three biggest month-over-month changes."*


We ran that exact prompt in Claude. It returned a table covering November 2025 to October 2026 and flagged these changes:


- **October 2026** : Ranking keywords jumped 73%, to about 5.8 million, while traffic fell 16%
- **September 2026** : Ranking keywords rose 42%, while traffic fell 9%
- **May 2026** : Traffic rose 37%, to about 15 million, while ranking keywords stayed flat


The assistant also spotted a pattern: when keyword counts nearly double while traffic falls, the new keywords usually rank too low to send many visits. So before treating it as a real change, it suggested checking how those keywords are spread across ranking positions.


Pulling the same data by hand would mean switching the date in[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) 12 times. And because the data is already in the assistant, you can ask follow-up questions right away, like which pages drove the May jump or how a competitor compares over the same months.


What you can pull through MCP depends on your plan, so past-month data needs the same Guru-level access as in the Semrush interface (Semrush One Pro+ and up, or SEO Classic Guru and Business).


Every MCP query uses API units. In our tests, a year of monthly data for one domain cost about 120 units, or roughly 10 per month of data.


Semrush One Pro+ and SEO Classic Guru plans include 50,000 MCP API units, which reset on your renewal date. You can check your balance under " **My Profile** " > " **Subscription Info** ."


***Further reading*** *:*[How to Create an AI SEO Report](https://www.semrush.com/blog/create-ai-seo-search-marketing-report/)


### 10. Recover lost SEO data


Historical SEO data lets you rebuild a site's past SEO performance, including traffic trends, keyword rankings, and top pages, even if you no longer have access to the tools or analytics that tracked it.


That's useful when you inherit a site with no records, switch from another platform, or discover your analytics weren't set up correctly for months.


To recover that lost SEO data in Semrush, start in[Domain Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/overview/) :


1. Enter the domain
2. Set the chart range to " **All time** " and switch the view to " **Months** "
3. Review estimated organic traffic in the "Traffic" chart and ranking keywords in the "Keywords" chart, which splits them by position (top 3, 4-10, 11-20, 21-50, and 51-100) and shows AI Overview appearances
4. Use the date selector at the top of the page to open any past month, then scroll down to see that month's top keywords, SERP features, keyword intent, and position distribution


Repeat step 4 for each month you need to rebuild your SEO timeline. You can also export the chart data with the " **Export** " button.


If you're moving to Semrush from another rank tracker, you can also bring your existing ranking history with you. Annual Guru and Business subscribers can import historical rankings from several other rank tracking platforms, so your[Position Tracking](https://www.semrush.com/position-tracking/) history doesn't start from zero.


## Start building your SEO history now


SEO data without history is a guess. History tells you whether a change needs action or just patience.


A traffic drop might be your problem, or every site in your niche might have felt it. A keyword might be growing, or it might just be October. A page might have gotten worse, or the SERP around it might have changed.


Semrush historical data gives you the "before" for any site or keyword, going back years. Position Tracking and Prompt Tracking give you your own detailed history, but only from the day you start them.


[Try Semrush](https://www.semrush.com/signup/) to start tracking your data and put your history to work.


## Semrush historical data FAQs


### Is Semrush data reliable?


Yes, Semrush data is reliable for spotting trends and patterns. Historical SEO data shows estimated monthly figures, so use it to see direction and turning points, and rely on your own analytics for exact numbers.


### Where does Semrush get its data?


Semrush gets its SEO data from search results collected through third-party providers, a clickstream panel used to estimate traffic, and its own backlink crawler. Machine learning combines these sources into the metrics you see in each tool. Learn more in our[knowledge base article on Semrush data](https://www.semrush.com/kb/997-semrush-data) .


### How often is Semrush data updated?


Semrush updates keyword data anywhere from daily to monthly, depending on how popular the keyword is. Updates for smaller regional databases can take a little longer.


### Can I export keyword ranking history?


Yes, you can export keyword ranking history from[Organic Rankings](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/organic/overview/) to Excel or CSV. Export a past month's data whenever you want a permanent record of where you stood.


### Where can I find historical market data?


Historical market data is in the[Semrush Traffic & Market Toolkit](https://www.semrush.com/kb/1505-getting-started-with-traffic-and-market) , which has monthly data back to January 2017. It requires a separate Traffic & Market Toolkit subscription.


### Who owns Semrush?


Adobe owns Semrush.[Adobe completed its acquisition of Semrush on April 28, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000796343/000079634326000112/adbe-20260529.htm) .


### What are examples of historical SEO data?


Examples of historical SEO data include a domain's estimated organic traffic over time, the keywords it ranked for in a past month, past search volume and Keyword Difficulty for a keyword, and the SERP features that appeared for a search in the past. In Semrush, you'll find these in Domain Overview, Organic Rankings, Keyword Overview, and Top Pages.
